title: Chennai's Poppadum Turns Jain Food Into Playful Street-Food Adventure
excerpt: The Kilpauk vegetarian diner's new Jain menu runs from Indori bhutte ka kees and pav bhaji quesadillas to a Military Hotel-style potlam biriyani — all without onion, garlic or root vegetables.
body:
• Poppadum, the inventive vegetarian diner in Chennai's Kilpauk neighbourhood, has launched a dedicated Jain menu that stretches from Indori bhutte ka kees and pav bhaji quesadillas to a Military Hotel-style potlam biriyani.
  • Highlights include Shetty's paneer tikka, Dilli wale momos with a homemade Jain momo chutney, edamame dabeli and a bowl-shaped crispy rumali roti — all cooked without onion, garlic or root vegetables.
  • The mains run from Bhopali paneer rezala and Lahori saag chhole to an Alleppey vegetable masala, mopped up with mirch masala laccha roti and butter naan.
  • Reader utility: a meal for two costs ₹1,800++ at Poppadum, 12/3A Ormes Road, Kilpauk, Chennai, open Tuesday to Sunday, noon to 3 pm and 7 to 11 pm.

Jain food has a reputation problem. The rules are strict — no onion, no garlic, no root vegetables — and many diners assume the result must be plain by definition. A newly launched Jain menu at Poppadum, the inventive vegetarian diner in Chennai's Kilpauk neighbourhood, is built to dismantle that assumption, according to Indulge Express, treating street food as raw material for something playful rather than a boundary.

The review describes a meal that opens with Indori bhutte ka kees — creamy corn, jeeravan masala and crisp kataifi that eats almost like a chaat — and Shetty's paneer tikka, soft enough to cut through, carrying a gentle smoky richness from ghee under a warm red chilli and curry leaf masala, with raw mango chutney pulling it together.

Context & Background

Poppadum is itself only a few months old. It opened in Kilpauk on May 29, 2026, spread across 2,200 sq ft with seating for 60 guests, according to Indian Retailer, with a concept centred on reinterpreting regional Indian cuisine through contemporary presentation and familiar flavours. Founder Abbas Shahzad has said the goal is not to reinvent Indian food but "to make you experience it differently for a moment."

The Jain menu is the latest turn of that idea. The Dilli wale momos arrive with a green pea and water chestnut filling and a homemade Jain momo chutney that keeps the dumplings lively, while the pav bhaji quesadilla puts Bombay tawa masala and melted mozzarella inside a toasted tortilla with tomato-pepper salsa. An edamame dabeli arrives looking like a paav, layered with masala peanuts, spicy Rajkot chutney, pomegranate and sev, and the crispy rumali roti is shaped, almost comically, like a bowl, filled with green mango and corn kachumber.

The mains continue the cross-country route: Bhopali paneer rezala with roasted pumpkin and malai cashew, a deeper, earthier Lahori saag chhole with spinach, chickpeas, spicy yoghurt masala and burnt cumin, and an Alleppey vegetable masala built on tomato, coconut, raw mango and crispy curry leaves. A five-lentil Poppadum daal tadka sits beside them, familiar and reassuring. The night, per the review, ends with the slightly spicy Military Hotel potlam biriyani, cooked with fragrant jeeraga samba rice, baby corn and green masala.

Impact & Analysis

The menu matters beyond the novelty of its dishes. Chennai has a large Jain community, drawn substantially from Marwari, Gujarati and Rajasthani merchant families, and its dining options have historically skewed towards traditional thalis and home-style cooking. A full Jain menu at a contemporary, design-forward restaurant signals that dietary-observant dining is becoming a commercial proposition rather than an afterthought — a niche with real spending power is being courted with the same creativity as any other.

It also fits a wider pattern in Indian restaurants, where constraint is being sold as creativity. Jain, satvik and no-onion-no-garlic formats give chefs a defined rulebook to play against, and the results — a quesadilla that reads as pav bhaji, a dabeli rebuilt around edamame — tend to travel well on social media, which is where modern restaurant reputations are increasingly made.

"The goal isn't to reinvent Indian food. It's to make you experience it differently for a moment."

— Abbas Shahzad, Founder, Poppadum

Diaspora Angle

For the Jain diaspora in the US, UK and the Gulf — and for any NRI heading home — the development is a useful data point about how quickly India's dining scene is professionalising around dietary observance. Eating out while keeping Jain rules has traditionally meant compromise or cooking at home; menus like this one suggest the next Chennai visit could include a restaurant meal that needs no explanation at the table.

What's Next

The Jain menu is on now at Poppadum, 12/3A Ormes Road, Kilpauk, open Tuesday to Sunday for lunch from noon to 3 pm and dinner from 7 to 11 pm, at ₹1,800++ for two. With the festival season approaching, it will be worth watching whether the restaurant extends the experiment — a Diwali-season Jain tasting menu would be the obvious next move for a kitchen that has already shown it enjoys a constraint.
